This is a *lost update*, and nobody was told. (Writing the same file at the same instant can also interleave the bytes of two jobs, which is worse. We were lucky here: the threads mostly took turns.)

Now the worse case. One job rewrites a big file, which takes about 10 seconds. While it is still writing, a reader opens the file. Then the machine "crashes" (we kill the job) halfway:

```{python}
rewrite = """
import pyarrow.parquet as pq
pq.write_table(pq.read_table('covid_big.parquet'), 'shared.parquet', compression='zstd')
"""

writer = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, "-c", rewrite])   # start rewriting shared.parquet
time.sleep(4)                                                 # let it get partway through
try:
    pq.read_table("shared.parquet")                           # a reader opens it mid-write
except Exception as e:
    print("reader:", e)
writer.kill()                                                 # the crash
writer.wait()
print(os.path.getsize("shared.parquet"), "bytes left behind")
```

```{python}
#| error: true
pq.read_table("shared.parquet")                               # try to use the file afterwards
```

The error is `Parquet magic bytes not found in footer. Either the file is corrupted or this is not a parquet file.` A Parquet file ends with its footer (the metadata that says where everything is), and the footer is written last. A file whose writer stopped early has no footer, so the whole file is unreadable. All the data that did get written is useless, and the good file that used to be there was already overwritten. The same error is what a reader sees if it arrives while the writer is working. A database never shows a reader a half-finished change: it writes a log first, and a crash is undone when it restarts. We see this below.

```bash
rm shared.parquet #cleanup
```

**4. Types, but no rules.** Parquet knows that `cases` is an integer, which a CSV does not. But it knows nothing about what values *make sense*: nothing refuses a negative `cases`, a `state` that is not a state, or the same county and date appearing twice. The writer decides, and nobody checks it when the data arrives.

Let us put three pieces of nonsense into the data (a negative `cases`, a `state` called "Israel" and a repeated row) and write it to Parquet:

```{r}
library(arrow)
library(dplyr)

setwd("~/workspace/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026/scratch/lec03")

df <- read_csv_arrow("covid.csv", col_types = schema(fips = string()))
df$cases[1] <- -5000L                 # nonsense example 1: negative cases
df$state[2] <- "Israel"               # nonsense example 2: not an American state
df <- bind_rows(df, df[3, ])          # nonsense example 3: the same county and date twice
write_parquet(df, "bad.parquet")      # it writes the nonsense permanently to the dataset without throwing any error

bad <- read_parquet("bad.parquet")
bad |> slice(c(1, 2, 3, n())) |> select(date, county, state, cases)
```

Parquet wrote all of it without a single warning, and it will hand it back to the next person who reads the file. Compare what Postgres does with a bad row in "The database checks your data" below.

```bash
rm bad.parquet
```

**5. Combining tables.** Adding each state's population to every row needs a second table and a program that can join them. Parquet only stores the tables; the joining is left to whichever tool reads them.

**6. Relationships between tables.** Suppose counties live in one table and their cases in another. Nothing in Parquet knows that every row of the second must point to a row of the first, so you can delete a county and leave its cases behind, or add cases for a county that does not exist. A database can state this rule once (a *foreign key*) and then refuse to break it.

**7. Reading a whole row.** Parquet stores each column in its own block, which is wonderful for adding up one column and poor for fetching *everything* about one record (for example, one customer's name, address, orders and balance for a web page). Assembling a single row means reading from every column's block. A database stores rows together and, with an index, goes straight there.

**8. Changing the schema.** To add a column or change a type, you rewrite every file. If you only rewrite some of them, the files now disagree and every reader has to cope with the mix. A database changes the definition of the table once (`ALTER TABLE`) and handles the old rows itself.

**9. Who may see what.** A Parquet file is a file, so permissions are all-or-nothing: whoever can open it can read every column and every row. A database has users and roles, and can allow one person to see only some tables, columns or rows, and another to change them. That matters as soon as a table holds anything private.

**10. Deleting data.** Privacy rules (such as the GDPR "right to be forgotten") require you to remove one person's records on request. In Parquet that means rewriting the files that contain them, and the old copies in backups and downloads are still there. In a database it is a single `DELETE`, and the history is managed in one place.

**11. Backups, history and recovery.** If a bad job overwrites a Parquet file, the old version is gone unless somebody remembered to copy it, and nothing records who changed what. A database keeps a log of every change, so it can restore the data to the state it had at any chosen minute, and can copy itself to a second machine continuously in case the first one dies.

Parquet is not to blame here. It was never meant to do all these jobs!! It is just a *file format* for storing a table well, and everything on this list is a service that a *database* provides on top of storing the table.

## Databases!

### A short history

+-----------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Year      | What happened                                                                                |
+:==========+:=============================================================================================+
| 1970      | **Edgar Codd** at IBM publishes "A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks":    |
|           | store data in tables (relations) and ask for it by *what* you want, not by how to find it.   |
|           | Until then, databases were tangled networks of pointers that programmers navigated by hand.  |
+-----------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| 1974-79   | IBM builds **System R** (no related to the statistical language R) and invents the query     |
|           | language that becomes **SQL**. At Berkeley, **Michael Stonebraker** builds                   |
|           | **Ingres**, a second relational system.                                                      |
+-----------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| 1977-79   | **Larry Ellison** founds the company that becomes **Oracle**, and in 1979 it sells the first |
|           | commercial SQL database. IBM's **DB2** follows in 1983.                                      |
+-----------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| 1986-87   | SQL becomes an ANSI standard (and an ISO standard a year later), so queries move between     |
|           | products. Stonebraker starts **Postgres** ("post-Ingres") at Berkeley.                       |
+-----------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| 1989      | **Microsoft SQL Server** ships, built with Sybase.                                           |
+-----------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| 1995      | **MySQL** is released by a small Swedish company and, being free and easy, becomes the       |
|           | database behind the early web, the "LAMP" stack (Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP/Perl/Python).     |
|           | Facebook, Wikipedia, Flickr, Yahoo and Slashdot all started on it, as did WordPress, which   |
|           | still powers about 40% of websites.                                                          |
+-----------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| 1996      | Postgres gets SQL support and is renamed **PostgreSQL**. It stays open-source and            |
|           | community-owned.                                                                             |
+-----------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| 2000      | **SQLite**: a database that is just one file, with no server at all. It ends up inside every |
|           | phone and web browser.                                                                       |
+-----------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| 2009-10   | The **NoSQL** wave (**MongoDB**, **Redis**, Cassandra) trades some of SQL's guarantees for   |
|           | easier scaling. Oracle buys Sun, and with it MySQL, so MySQL's creators fork it as           |
|           | **MariaDB**.                                                                                 |
+-----------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| 2010s     | Cloud warehouses appear (BigQuery, Redshift, Snowflake) that run SQL over columnar data, the |
|           | same idea as Parquet. Most NoSQL systems then add SQL back.                                  |
+-----------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| 2019      | **DuckDB** appears: SQLite's "just a file" idea, but for analytics, and it queries Parquet   |
|           | directly.                                                                                    |
+-----------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

: Dates are from my memory of each project's history; check before quoting one.

### Who uses what?

Nobody counts the users of a database, because most are free to download and run anywhere. The best public number is the annual **Stack Overflow Developer Survey**, which asked developers which databases they had done extensive development work with in the past year. (Developers could name several, so the percentages add up to more than 100%.)

+----------------------+-------------+------------------------------------------+---------------------+
| Database             | Born        | Who makes it                             | Developers using it |
+:=====================+:============+:=========================================+====================:+
| PostgreSQL           | 1986 (1996) | open-source community                    | 55.6%               |
+----------------------+-------------+------------------------------------------+---------------------+
| MySQL                | 1995        | Oracle (since 2010)                      | 40.5%               |
+----------------------+-------------+------------------------------------------+---------------------+
| SQLite               | 2000        | D. Richard Hipp's small team             | 37.5%               |
+----------------------+-------------+------------------------------------------+---------------------+
| Microsoft SQL Server | 1989        | Microsoft                                | 30.1%               |
+----------------------+-------------+------------------------------------------+---------------------+
| Redis                | 2009        | Redis Ltd. (key-value store, not SQL)    | 28.0%               |
+----------------------+-------------+------------------------------------------+---------------------+
| MongoDB              | 2009        | MongoDB Inc. (document store, not SQL)   | 24.0%               |
+----------------------+-------------+------------------------------------------+---------------------+
| MariaDB              | 2009        | MariaDB Foundation (a fork of MySQL)     | 22.5%               |
+----------------------+-------------+------------------------------------------+---------------------+
| Oracle               | 1979        | Oracle                                   | 10.6%               |
+----------------------+-------------+------------------------------------------+---------------------+

: Share of all respondents of the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey (<https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2025/technology>). Oracle is a big earner but is used by a small fraction of developers: it is common inside big companies and rare in new projects.

PostgreSQL has been the most used for a few years now, which is one reason we use it here. Everything we do in this unit is standard SQL and works, with small changes, in all of the relational systems above.

We will use **PostgreSQL** ("Postgres"), which you installed in the setup guide.
